title: Opaque probe resolution runbook with Terraform safe-apply
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description: Create a pragmatic runbook and safe automated remediation pipeline for the three most common opaque Private (VPC) health-check failures we see in production: probe timeouts (kube liveness/readiness), KV cache corruption leading to token errors, and intermittent control-plane API errors. The goal is to codify detection rules, triage heuristics, Terraform-driven corrective actions with dry-run gates, and a minimal human-in-loop approval for high-risk changes (networking, IAM, or k8s node replacement).
acceptance_criteria: Runbook documents deterministic triage steps for timeout, kv cache, and control-plane errors
Automated remediation implements a Terraform-driven safe-apply flow that defaults to plan-only and can escalate to apply under configured conditions
Remediation has circuit breakers: do-not-apply tag for production, auto-rollback on increased 5xx rates, and manual approval path for networking/IAM changes
Observed remediation played out in a staging incident and captured in postmortem with metrics showing reduced MTTR
CI tests validate terraform module idempotency and dry-run outputs for the three failure classes
runbook_steps: Detection: alert fires (vpc-probe-timeout / kvcache-error / controlplane-5xx) from Console synthetic probes or private-agent heartbeats
Initial triage: capture last 15m of node heartbeats, kube events, terraform-state drift, and API gateway 504/502 logs
Classification: use rule set to classify as TIMEOUT | KVCACHE | CONTROLPLANE; if ambiguous escalate to on-call
Quick mitigation: for TIMEOUT -> temporarily route traffic to warm fallback model variant; for KVCACHE -> mark affected shard readonly; for CONTROLPLANE -> switch region fallback per routing policy
Gather artifacts: attach terraform plan (auto-generated), k8s pod logs, node metrics, and the private-agent debug bundle to the incident
automated_remediation_flow: Step A - Preflight: run terraform plan with -out=plan.tfout and collect plan diff artifact. Validate that planned changes are limited to known safe modules (node-replace, kube-probe-restart, kvcache-clear). Reject plan if changes include networking or IAM unless explicit flag provided.

Step B - Safety gates: evaluate metrics window (5m and 30m). Allow automated apply only if 5m-error-rate > 3x baseline AND 30m-error-rate trending up AND no active deploy pipelines. Otherwise record plan and open manual approval ticket.

Step C - Apply: if gates pass, run terraform apply -auto-approve on a single-target module (module.vpc_node_replacer module or module.kvcache_repair). Use canary: apply to 1 host/shard, wait 10 minutes health window, then roll remaining targets.

Step D - Post-apply validation: run synthetic probe and canary traffic for 15 minutes. If 5xx or probe failures increase vs baseline, trigger automatic rollback (apply saved plan reverse) and open incident for manual investigation.
Step E - Audit and telemetry: publish plan, apply logs, and outcome to Console incident workspace and append terraform state diff to the incident notes
rollback_plan: If automated apply causes increased error rates beyond threshold, immediately run terraform apply using saved pre-apply state snapshot to revert targets
If revert fails, isolate traffic to secondary region/fallback model and mark the private deployment as degraded in status page
If IAM or network change is implicated and cannot be rolled back automatically, escalate to SRE lead and cloud-networking owner with on-call paging
testing_and_validation: Create a staging harness that injects each failure class (kube probe timeout, kvcache corruption, control-plane 5xx) and validates that the plan produced changes are scoped and safe
E2E test: run full safe-apply in staging with canary target and validate metric windows, rollback behavior, and artifact collection
Unit tests for terraform modules: plan-only asserts, idempotency checks, and mock state drift scenarios
Chaos test: random node restart during canary window to ensure rollback retains cluster stability
